code.title: INNER, LEFT, RIGHT and FULL join row counts
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE customers(id INT, name TEXT);
CREATE TABLE orders(id INT, customer_id INT);
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'Asha'),(2,'Ben'),(3,'Cy'),(4,'Dee');
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (10,1),(11,1),(12,2),(13,9),(14,8);
""")
def show(title, sql):
    rows = db.execute(sql).fetchall()
    print(title, len(rows), "rows:", rows)

# INNER: only matching pairs
show("INNER", "SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id")
# LEFT: every customer, NULL when no order
show("LEFT ", "SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id")
# RIGHT = LEFT with the tables swapped (works on every SQLite version)
show("RIGHT", "SELECT c.name, o.id FROM orders o LEFT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id=c.id")
# FULL = LEFT rows + the right-only rows
show("FULL ", """SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id
 UNION ALL SELECT NULL, o.id FROM orders o
 WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM customers c WHERE c.id=o.customer_id)""")

followUps:
Yes, always: swap the two tables and change RIGHT to LEFT. A RIGHT JOIN B ON ... returns the same rows as B LEFT JOIN A ON ..., only with the column order of the tables swapped. Example: customers (4 rows) RIGHT JOIN orders (5 rows) keeps all 5 orders, exactly like orders LEFT JOIN customers.

Most teams write only LEFT joins because reading top to bottom, the first table is the one you keep, which is easier to follow. Some engines, such as old SQLite, do not even offer RIGHT or FULL.

An INNER JOIN can, because it keeps only pairs that match. If table A has 1,000 rows and table B has 500 rows but only 20 keys match, the result has 20 rows, fewer than either input.

An INNER JOIN can also return more rows than either input when one key matches many rows (one customer with 100 orders gives 100 rows). LEFT, RIGHT and FULL joins never return fewer rows than their preserved side, so only INNER (and semi/anti joins) can shrink below both inputs.

code.title: Condition in ON vs WHERE in a LEFT JOIN

followUps:
Because the OR rescues only the rows with no match at all, not the rows that matched but failed the test. Example: customers Asha (order with x = 1), Cy (one order with x = 2) and Dee (no orders). The LEFT JOIN pads Dee with NULLs, so b.x = 1 OR b.id IS NULL keeps Asha and Dee, but Cy is dropped.

With the condition in ON (ON b.cust = a.id AND b.x = 1) Cy is kept too, NULL-padded. It also breaks if b.id can be NULL for other reasons.

Look at the plan: if the optimizer sees a WHERE filter that rejects NULLs on the optional table, it rewrites the LEFT JOIN as an INNER JOIN, and EXPLAIN shows an inner join (PostgreSQL prints Hash Join rather than Hash Left Join; SQL Server shows an inner join operator).

So if you wrote LEFT but the plan says inner, a WHERE condition on the optional side is cancelling it. Compare row counts too: the LEFT version should never have fewer rows than the left table.

code.title: Self join: employees earning more than their manager
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE employees(emp_id INT, name TEXT, salary INT, manager_id INT);
INSERT INTO employees VALUES
 (1,'CEO',300,NULL),(2,'Mia',250,1),(3,'Raj',260,2),(4,'Li',200,2),
 (5,'Tom',250,2),(6,'Zed',NULL,2),(7,'Orphan',500,99);
""")
print(db.execute("SELECT * FROM employees").fetchall())
# Self join: the same table plays employee (e) and manager (m)
sql = """SELECT e.name, e.salary, m.name, m.salary
         FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON m.emp_id = e.manager_id
         WHERE e.salary > m.salary"""
print("earn more than manager:", db.execute(sql).fetchall())
# Tom ties Mia (strict >), Zed has NULL salary, CEO and Orphan have no manager row
# Reversed ON answers the opposite question (managers earning more than their reports)
bad = sql.replace("m.emp_id = e.manager_id", "e.emp_id = m.manager_id")
print("reversed ON:", db.execute(bad).fetchall())

followUps:
Join the employees table a third time: the manager's manager is the manager of m. Use a LEFT JOIN if you want people without a grandmanager too.

SELECT e.name, m.name AS mgr, g.name AS grand
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON m.emp_id = e.manager_id
LEFT JOIN employees g ON g.emp_id = m.manager_id;

For an unlimited depth you need a recursive CTE instead of a fixed number of self joins.

Use a recursive CTE that walks up the chain from every employee, then compare each salary with the maximum salary of all ancestors.

WITH RECURSIVE up(emp, anc) AS (
 SELECT emp_id, manager_id FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL
 UNION ALL SELECT u.emp, m.manager_id FROM up u JOIN employees m ON m.emp_id=u.anc WHERE m.manager_id IS NOT NULL)
SELECT e.name FROM employees e JOIN up ON up.emp=e.emp_id JOIN employees a ON a.emp_id=up.anc
GROUP BY e.emp_id HAVING e.salary > MAX(a.salary);

Cost is O(N x depth). Employees with no ancestors are excluded.

code.title: NOT IN with a NULL vs NOT EXISTS
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE a(x INT);  CREATE TABLE b(y INT);
INSERT INTO a VALUES (1),(2),(3);
INSERT INTO b VALUES (1),(NULL);
""")
def run(t, sql): print(t, db.execute(sql).fetchall())
# 2 <> 1 AND 2 <> NULL -> UNKNOWN, so no row survives
run("NOT IN          ", "SELECT x FROM a WHERE x NOT IN (SELECT y FROM b)")
# NOT EXISTS: a NULL never matches, so 2 and 3 are correctly returned
run("NOT EXISTS      ", "SELECT x FROM a WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM b WHERE b.y = a.x)")
run("LEFT JOIN NULL  ", "SELECT a.x FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON b.y=a.x WHERE b.y IS NULL")
run("NOT IN + filter ", "SELECT x FROM a WHERE x NOT IN (SELECT y FROM b WHERE y IS NOT NULL)")

followUps:
No. A positive IN is safe: x IN (1, NULL) is TRUE when x = 1 and UNKNOWN otherwise, and WHERE treats UNKNOWN as not a match, which is the result you want anyway. NULL never causes a wrong row to appear.

The danger is only with NOT IN, where UNKNOWN is negated into UNKNOWN again instead of becoming TRUE. Example: 2 IN (1, NULL) is UNKNOWN, 2 NOT IN (1, NULL) is also UNKNOWN, so the row is dropped.

On a modern optimizer they are usually the same: both become an anti-join, and with an index on the join key both are fast. NOT EXISTS is the safe default because it has the right NULL meaning.

Differences show up in details: a LEFT JOIN anti-join builds all the joined rows before filtering in some plans, and it is easy to test the wrong column for NULL. Always check with EXPLAIN on real data; if both give the same plan, choose by readability.

code.title: Semi-join with EXISTS vs JOIN + DISTINCT

followUps:
IN is clearer when you compare against a short fixed list or a simple one-column subquery, such as status IN ('paid','shipped') or id IN (SELECT id FROM vip). It reads like plain English and needs no correlation.

EXISTS is clearer when the match needs several columns or extra conditions, for example EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.total > 100). Performance is normally identical, so pick the more readable one.

A hash semi join builds a hash table of the distinct join keys from B, then scans A once: if A's key is found in the table, output the A row and move on, never output it twice.

Example: B has keys {1, 1, 3}, the table holds {1, 3}; A rows with keys 1, 2, 3 return rows 1 and 3. Cost is about O(|A| + |B|) time and O(distinct keys of B) memory, and each A row appears at most once, so no DISTINCT is needed.

code.title: Fan-out doubles revenue after a join; aggregate first
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE orders(id INT, amount INT);
CREATE TABLE payments(id INT, order_id INT, paid INT);
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,100),(2,50);
INSERT INTO payments VALUES (1,1,60),(2,1,40),(3,2,50);
""")
def run(t, sql): print(t, db.execute(sql).fetchall())
run("true revenue   ", "SELECT SUM(amount) FROM orders")
# Fan-out: order 1 has 2 payments so its amount is counted twice (100+100+50)
run("after join     ", "SELECT SUM(o.amount) FROM orders o JOIN payments p ON p.order_id=o.id")
# Diagnose: join key must be unique on the payments side
run("dup check      ", "SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) FROM payments GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*)>1")
# Fix: aggregate payments to one row per order first, then join 1:1
run("fixed          ", """WITH p AS (SELECT order_id, SUM(paid) paid FROM payments GROUP BY order_id)
                          SELECT SUM(o.amount), SUM(p.paid) FROM orders o LEFT JOIN p ON p.order_id=o.id""")

followUps:
COUNT(DISTINCT) is legitimate when you want to count unique things, such as the number of distinct customers who ordered, and you accept that each is counted once regardless of how many rows they produced after a join.

It is not a fix for a doubled SUM. Example: orders 100 and 50, order 1 has two payments. COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) correctly gives 2 orders, but SUM(DISTINCT o.amount) would also wrongly collapse two different orders with the same amount of 50.

A fan trap is a one-to-many join that repeats rows of the "one" side, multiplying its measures (orders joined to payments). A chasm trap is when two separate one-to-many branches hang off the same table (orders to payments and orders to shipments), so rows multiply across the branches: 2 payments x 3 shipments = 6 rows per order.

BI tools avoid both by aggregating each fact table to the shared key separately, then joining the results (Looker symmetric aggregates, Tableau relationships, Power BI one-direction filters).

code.title: Orders without customers and customers without orders
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE customers(customer_id INT, name TEXT);
CREATE TABLE orders(order_id INT, customer_id INT);
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'Asha'),(2,'Ben'),(3,'Cy');
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (10,1),(11,2),(12,NULL),(13,99);
""")
# FULL OUTER JOIN emulated as two anti-joins glued with UNION ALL (no duplicates possible)
sql = """
SELECT 'customer without orders' AS issue, c.customer_id AS key, NULL AS order_id
  FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id=c.customer_id)
UNION ALL
SELECT CASE WHEN o.customer_id IS NULL THEN 'guest order (NULL id)'
            ELSE 'orphan order (deleted customer)' END, o.customer_id, o.order_id
  FROM orders o WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM customers c WHERE c.customer_id=o.customer_id)
"""
for r in db.execute(sql): print(r)
# Why not UNION: it would also de-duplicate genuinely repeated rows

followUps:
UNION removes duplicate rows, which silently deletes genuine ones: two orphan orders with identical selected values (say both with customer id 99 and the same label) collapse into one, so you under-count problems. It also needs a sort or hash step.

UNION ALL of two disjoint anti-joins cannot produce duplicates between the parts (a row is either a customer without orders or an order without customer), so it is both correct and cheaper.

Put the query in a scheduled job (cron, Airflow, dbt test) that runs daily and fails or alerts when the count is above zero. Save the offending rows, or at least their counts, into a table with the run date so you can watch the trend.

SELECT COUNT(*) AS bad_rows FROM ( ...the query... ) t;
-- alert if bad_rows > 0

Better still, fix the cause with a foreign key constraint so orphans cannot be inserted at all.

code.title: Missing join condition gives a Cartesian product
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE a(id INT); CREATE TABLE b(id INT, a_id INT);
INSERT INTO a VALUES (1),(2),(3);
INSERT INTO b VALUES (10,1),(11,1),(12,2),(13,3),(14,3);
""")
def count(sql): return db.execute(sql).fetchone()[0]
print("rows in a:", count("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM a"), " rows in b:", count("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM b"))
good = count("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM a JOIN b ON b.a_id=a.id")
bad = count("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM a, b")          # forgot the condition
print("with condition:", good)
print("no condition  :", bad, "(= 3 x 5)")
# Detect: compare to the expected size; a cartesian result equals |A| * |B|
print("looks cartesian?", bad == 3 * 5)
for row in db.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM a, b"): print("plan:", row[3])

followUps:
It is useful when you need every pairing: sizes x colours for a product catalogue (3 sizes x 4 colours = 12 variants), a calendar scaffold of dates x stores, or a one-row config table attached to each row. Generated on purpose, it is clean and predictable.

Always check the sizes first: 1 million rows x 1 million rows is 10^12 rows. Write CROSS JOIN explicitly so the next reader knows it was intended.

Multiply the sizes of the tables that are not tied together by a condition. Example: A has 1,000 rows, B 2,000 and C 500, and the A-to-B condition is missing. A x B is 2,000,000 rows before C is applied, and if C joins B on a key matching 1 row per B row, the final result is still about 2,000,000 rows instead of about 2,000.

Compare with the expected size: a result in the millions where you expected thousands is the warning sign.

code.title: Nested loop vs hash vs merge join
code.python:
import sqlite3
a = [(i, i % 5) for i in range(8)]          # (id, key)
b = [(k, "row%d" % k) for k in range(5)]    # (key, label)
print("A:", a); print("B:", b)
# Nested loop: for each outer row scan the whole inner list -> O(N*M)
nl = [(x[0], y[1]) for x in a for y in b if x[1] == y[0]]
# Hash join: build a dict on the smaller input, probe with the other -> O(N+M)
table = {y[0]: y[1] for y in b}
hj = [(x[0], table[x[1]]) for x in a if x[1] in table]
# Merge join: sort both on the key, advance pointers (b keys unique here)
sa, sb = sorted(a, key=lambda r: r[1]), sorted(b)
mj, j = [], 0
for x in sa:
    while sb[j][0] < x[1]: j += 1
    if sb[j][0] == x[1]: mj.append((x[0], sb[j][1]))
print("same result:", sorted(nl) == sorted(hj) == sorted(mj), "rows:", len(nl))
print("comparisons: nested loop", len(a) * len(b), "hash probes", len(a))
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("CREATE TABLE a(id INT,k INT); CREATE TABLE b(k INT,label TEXT);")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO a VALUES (?,?)", a); db.executemany("INSERT INTO b VALUES (?,?)", b)
print("sqlite rows:", len(db.execute("SELECT * FROM a JOIN b ON a.k=b.k").fetchall()))

followUps:
Nested loop and hash join can do FULL OUTER JOIN only with extra tracking: the engine remembers which rows of each side matched and, at the end, emits the unmatched rows padded with NULLs. Merge join handles FULL naturally because both sorted inputs are walked together, and a row that finds no partner is emitted at once.

Many engines (PostgreSQL, SQL Server) support FULL only for hash and merge joins, because a plain nested loop would need that tracking for the inner side. MySQL has no FULL JOIN at all.

Without an index on the foreign key, every outer row forces a scan of the whole child table. With N outer rows and M child rows that is N x M comparisons; with an index each probe costs about log M.

Example: 10,000 customers and 5,000,000 orders. Unindexed that is 5 x 10^10 comparisons, indexed roughly 10,000 x 23 = 230,000 steps. The index also makes deleting a parent row fast, because the database must check for child rows.

code.title: Relational division: students who took all required courses
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE students(id INT, name TEXT);
CREATE TABLE required(course_id INT);
CREATE TABLE enrollments(student_id INT, course_id INT);
INSERT INTO students VALUES (1,'Asha'),(2,'Ben'),(3,'Cy');
INSERT INTO required VALUES (101),(102);
INSERT INTO enrollments VALUES (1,101),(1,102),(1,101),(1,200),(2,101),(3,102),(3,101);
""")
# Double NOT EXISTS: no required course exists that the student has not taken
q1 = """SELECT s.name FROM students s WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM required r WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id=s.id AND e.course_id=r.course_id))"""
# Counting: join to the required set only, DISTINCT guards duplicate enrollments
q2 = """SELECT s.name FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id=s.id
  JOIN required r ON r.course_id=e.course_id GROUP BY s.id
  HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT e.course_id) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM required)"""
print("not exists:", db.execute(q1).fetchall())
print("counting  :", db.execute(q2).fetchall())
# Exactly the set: also no extra courses
q3 = q2 + " AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrollments x WHERE x.student_id=s.id AND x.course_id NOT IN (SELECT course_id FROM required))"
print("exactly   :", db.execute(q3).fetchall())

followUps:
Use the counting version and add a second condition that the student has no course outside the required set, or compare counts both ways: the student's number of distinct courses must equal the number of required courses and every one of them must be required.

SELECT student_id FROM enrollments
GROUP BY student_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT course_id) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM required)
 AND SUM(course_id NOT IN (SELECT course_id FROM required)) = 0;

Student Asha took 101, 102 and 200, so she fails; Cy took only 101 and 102, so he passes.

Usually the counting version (join to the required set, GROUP BY, HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT)) is easier: it becomes one join plus one hash aggregate, with cost about O(N). Double NOT EXISTS is correct but is two nested anti-joins, and some optimizers handle it poorly for large tables.

Double NOT EXISTS is the one that handles an empty required list correctly: everyone qualifies vacuously, whereas the counting version compares with 0 and returns no one. Test both against your data and read the plans.

code.title: CROSS JOIN scaffold for zero-filled reports

followUps:
You use a recursive CTE or generate the dates with a numbers sequence, then CROSS JOIN with stores. Example with a recursive CTE:

WITH RECURSIVE d(day) AS (
 SELECT '2026-01-01'
 UNION ALL SELECT date(day,'+1 day') FROM d WHERE day < '2026-01-31')
SELECT day FROM d;

PostgreSQL has generate_series, SQL Server uses a recursive CTE or a calendar table. Many teams keep a permanent calendar table, which is simplest and fastest.

It is a join where the right side is a subquery or function that can use columns from the left row, so it runs once per left row. SQL Server calls it CROSS APPLY, PostgreSQL and MySQL 8 use CROSS JOIN LATERAL (or JOIN LATERAL ... ON true).

Typical use: the top 3 orders for each customer, CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT * FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id ORDER BY total DESC LIMIT 3) t. A normal subquery in FROM cannot see the left table, so LATERAL is needed.

code.title: LEFT JOIN then INNER JOIN trap
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE a(id INT); CREATE TABLE b(id INT, a_id INT); CREATE TABLE c(id INT, b_id INT, v TEXT);
INSERT INTO a VALUES (1),(2),(3);
INSERT INTO b VALUES (10,1),(11,2);
INSERT INTO c VALUES (100,10,'x');
""")
def run(t, sql): print(t, db.execute(sql).fetchall())
# Trap: INNER JOIN c refers to optional b, so rows with b = NULL are dropped
run("LEFT then INNER ", "SELECT a.id FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON b.a_id=a.id JOIN c ON c.b_id=b.id")
# Fix 1: LEFT JOIN every table hanging off the optional branch
run("LEFT, LEFT      ", "SELECT a.id, c.v FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON b.a_id=a.id LEFT JOIN c ON c.b_id=b.id")
# Fix 2: group the branch in parentheses and join it once
run("grouped branch  ", "SELECT a.id, bc.v FROM a LEFT JOIN (SELECT b.a_id, c.v FROM b JOIN c ON c.b_id=b.id) bc ON bc.a_id=a.id")
# Debug tip: print the row count after each step
run("count after b   ", "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON b.a_id=a.id")

followUps:
It is correct when the later table is truly required for the result: if the report means "only customers who have a shipped item", then dropping rows that cannot reach that table is the intended meaning, not a bug.

Example: customers LEFT JOIN orders INNER JOIN order_items. If the business question is "customers with at least one purchased item", rows without orders should go. The mistake is only when the INNER JOIN was added for convenience while the intent was to keep unmatched customers.

Outer joins are not associative, so reordering them can change the result. (A LEFT JOIN B) INNER JOIN C ON C.x = B.x removes A rows with no B, while A LEFT JOIN (B INNER JOIN C) keeps them NULL-padded.

Example: A has 3 rows, only A1 matches B, and B matches C. The first form returns 1 row, the second returns 3. Inner joins can be freely reordered, but once a LEFT or RIGHT join is involved you must keep the written order or use parentheses to say what you mean.

code.title: ON vs USING vs NATURAL JOIN
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE a(id INT, name TEXT); CREATE TABLE b(id INT, name TEXT, extra INT);
INSERT INTO a VALUES (1,'x'),(2,'y');
INSERT INTO b VALUES (1,'x',5),(2,'z',6);
""")
def run(t, sql):
    cur = db.execute(sql)
    print(t, [d[0] for d in cur.description], cur.fetchall())
run("ON     ", "SELECT * FROM a JOIN b ON a.id=b.id")      # both id columns kept
run("USING  ", "SELECT * FROM a JOIN b USING (id)")        # one merged id column
# NATURAL joins on ALL shared names (id AND name), so 'y' vs 'z' silently drops a row
run("NATURAL", "SELECT * FROM a NATURAL JOIN b")
# A new shared column added later would change NATURAL results without any code change
db.execute("ALTER TABLE a ADD COLUMN extra INT")
run("NATURAL after ALTER", "SELECT id, name FROM a NATURAL JOIN b")

followUps:
It depends on the engine, so do not rely on it. The SQL standard says a USING column has no table owner, so a.id may be rejected (PostgreSQL and MySQL accept it in some positions, SQL Server has no USING at all). The plain name id always works.

For portable code use ON and write a.id and b.id. For FULL JOIN, USING returns COALESCE(a.id, b.id) under the plain name.

NATURAL JOIN uses every shared column name, so adding a column with the same name to either table changes the join silently. Example: orders and customers join on customer_id today. Someone adds updated_at to both tables, and now the join also needs equal updated_at values, so almost every row disappears with no error.

Renaming or dropping a column can do the opposite and create a Cartesian product if no names are shared. Use explicit ON.

code.title: Index on the foreign key turns a scan into a seek
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE customers(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT, total INT);
""")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO customers VALUES (?,?)", [(i, "c%d" % i) for i in range(1, 1001)])
db.executemany("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (?,?,?)", [(i, i % 1000 + 1, i) for i in range(1, 5001)])
q = "SELECT c.name, o.total FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id=o.customer_id WHERE c.id=42"
def plan(t):
    print(t)
    for r in db.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN " + q): print("  ", r[3])
plan("without FK index:")
print("  rows:", len(db.execute(q).fetchall()))
# Index on the child-side foreign key turns the scan into a seek
db.execute("CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders(customer_id)")
db.execute("ANALYZE")
plan("with FK index:")
print("  rows:", len(db.execute(q).fetchall()))

followUps:
A broadcast join sends the whole small table to every node, so each node joins its local part of the big table with no movement of the big table. A shuffle join repartitions both tables by the join key so matching keys land on the same node, which costs network traffic for both.

Example: a 10 GB fact table with a 50 MB dimension: broadcast the 50 MB to 20 nodes (1 GB total traffic) instead of shuffling 10 GB. If both tables are large, shuffle (or co-partition ahead of time).

Denormalizing wins when a read is very frequent, the joined values rarely change, and the join cost is large. Copy the customer name into the orders table and a listing page needs no join at all.

The price is extra storage, writes that must update every copy, and risk of inconsistent values if an update is missed. Good cases: reporting tables, read-heavy dashboards and cached counters. Keep the normalized tables as the source of truth and rebuild the copy on a schedule or with triggers.
